summary: This RFC defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing a syslog process, the standard way systems record and forward log messages. Vendors that build syslog collectors can use it so that network management tools can configure logging in a consistent way across devices.

eli5.summary: Computers keep a diary of what happens to them. This gives a standard form for telling a computer how and where to write its diary, so every brand can be set up the same way.

questions: how to configure syslog with netconf
what is the ietf-syslog yang module
what is the default syslog tls port
subtitle: A standard YANG model for configuring where a device sends its log messages and which ones it keeps.

tldr.problem: Every vendor configures syslog its own way, so network management tools cannot set up logging consistently across different devices.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-syslog YANG module. It configures actions (console, log files, remote relays or collectors), each with a filter of facility and severity pairs and an optional regular expression, with optional features that vendors can pick from.
tldr.outcome: Tools using NETCONF or RESTCONF can configure syslog in a common way, and vendors can extend the model with their own features.

today: RFC 9742 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model (RFC 7950) for configuring the syslog feature running on a system. YANG models can be used with management protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) to install, change and delete the configuration of network devices. The model conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342).

A syslog process receives messages from the kernel, processes, applications or other syslog processes. It may log them to a local file, show them on the console, or relay them to syslog processes on other machines. What happens to a message depends on the facility that originated it and the severity assigned to it. Those definitions come from RFC 5424.

The model uses the YANG feature construct so that an implementation supports only the syslog features within its capabilities.
sections.eli5: Devices write down notes about what is going on. This document is a standard settings form for choosing which notes to keep and where to send them.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Three terms come from RFC 5424:

  • Originator: an entity that generates syslog content to be carried in a message.
  • Relay: an entity that forwards syslog messages. It accepts messages from originators or other relays and sends them to collectors or other relays.
  • Collector: an entity that gathers syslog content for further analysis.

This RFC adds one more: an action is the process that takes place for each syslog message received.
sections.eli5: An originator writes a note, a relay passes the note along, and a collector keeps it. An action is whatever the device does with each note.

sections.title: Design of the Syslog Model
sections.content:
The model was designed by comparing syslog features implemented by various vendors. It defines leafs common across implementations and keeps the design simple for flexibility. Because not every optional feature exists in every implementation, vendors use feature statements to say what they support, and they can also augment the model with proprietary features.

Messages flow from originators such as various components, the OS kernel, line cards, remote servers, SNMP events, interface events, a standby supervisor and syslog itself. They go to collectors, where filtering can take place. The collectors are configured in the actions container:

  • console
  • log files (file)
  • remote relays or collectors (remote)

The module is called ietf-syslog, and its top-level syslog container is a presence container that enables logging.
sections.eli5: Lots of parts of a device write notes. The settings choose three places the notes can go: the screen, a file, or another computer.

sections.title: Filtering by Facility, Severity and Pattern
sections.content:
Within each action, a selector filters messages. A selector is a list of one or more facility and severity pairs and, if the select-match feature is supported, an optional regular expression matched against the MSG field of the message (Section 6.4 of RFC 5424). If both a facility list and a pattern are given, both must match for a message to be selected.

The facility is a specific syslog facility or all facilities. The severity is one of the eight syslog severities, all, or none. none is a special case that can disable a filter. Severity numbers run from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug), and a lower value is a higher severity.

By default, a severity filter selects messages of the given severity and higher, shown in the model as equals-or-higher. With the select-adv-compare feature, the filter can instead pick a compare operation (equals or equals-or-higher) and an action: log, block (do not log) or stop (do not log and stop further processing). For example, compare equals with action block means messages with exactly that severity are not logged.

The facility list is ordered by the user. The module defines facilities with numerical codes 0 to 23, from kern (0) and user (1) through local0 (16) to local7 (23).
sections.eli5: Think of a sorting rule: "keep every note marked from the kitchen that is at least this important." You can also say "throw away notes that are exactly this important."

sections.title: Files and Remote Destinations
sections.content:
The file action holds a list of log files, each named with a URI (RFC 8089). It can use the structured-data feature and a file-rotation container with number-of-files, max-file-size, rollover and retention. The number-of-files leaf defaults to 1.

The remote action holds a list of destinations. For each, the user chooses a transport: UDP (RFC 5426) or TLS (RFC 5425). Several relays or collectors may be configured, but they have to use the same transport. The UDP port defaults to 514, and the TLS port to 6514, which the model notes was allocated as the default port for syslog over TLS. TLS parameters such as client identity, server authentication and keepalives come from the groupings of RFC 9645.

A remote destination can also override the facility, set a source interface, and, with the signed-messages feature, configure signed syslog messages (RFC 5848) with certificate signers, a hash algorithm and resend timers.
sections.eli5: Notes can be saved in files that get swapped out when they grow too big. They can also be mailed to another computer, either in a plain envelope (UDP) or a locked one (TLS).

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content: The RFC gives two examples written in XML. The first enables console logging for all facilities at severity critical. The second sends remote logs over UDP to foo.example.com for facility auth and severity error, in a destination named remote1.
sections.eli5: The examples fill out the form twice: once to show important problems on the screen, and once to mail login-related errors to another computer.

sections.title: Implementer Guidelines
sections.content:
Appendix B gives non-normative advice. Vendors often add facilities, and the RFC shows how to add them by defining identities that use syslog:syslog-facility as their base. Such extra facilities may not work with the syslog protocol of RFC 5424, so they apply to local syslog-like logging.

Terminal output needs more complex than the console subtree provides are expected to come from vendor extensions rather than the file subtree.

For file rotation, the RFC describes how an implementer might name files. When the active file reaches its maximum size or the rollover period passes, it can be closed, compressed and named <log-file/name>.0.gz, with older archives renumbered upward. The oldest can be overwritten when number-of-files is reached, and archives past the retention time can be removed. This is an informative guide only.
sections.eli5: If a vendor wants extra kinds of labels, there is a way to add them. Old log files can be squished into archives and numbered, and the oldest ones get thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed with YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF (RFC 8040), which have to use a secure transport layer and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content. The security considerations of RFC 9640 also apply.

All writable data nodes are likely to be sensitive, since unprotected writes can harm network operations. Two are singled out:

  • pattern-match: implementations MUST ensure the regular expression cannot cause a regular expression denial-of-service attack, where the pattern makes matching very slow.
  • signing/cert-signer: implementations MUST NOT specify a private key used for any other purpose.

Some readable nodes are sensitive too. The transport subtree reveals other hosts and services, and knowing that syslog (udp/514) is enabled on a host lets a malicious user spam that port. The signing subtree exposes signing properties, including certificate information. There are no particularly sensitive RPC or action operations.
sections.eli5: Because these settings decide where a device's diary goes, only trusted people should be allowed to change or read them, and a tricky search pattern must not be able to make the device freeze.
